newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Post-apartheid S.Africa moves on abortion reform.
newsitem.headline: Post-apartheid S.Africa moves on abortion reform.

text.p: The South African government, tackling one of the toughest moral issues of post-apartheid reform, proposed a draft law on Tuesday that would allow abortion on demand for women.
But, reflecting sensitivity on the issue, the proposed threshholds for allowing abortions were far more conservative than those approved by the government earlier this year.
The Termination of Pregnancy Bill published by Health Minister Nkosazana Zuma sees abortion on demand up to the 12th week of pregnancy and, under strict conditions, up to the 20th week.
A pregnant girl under the age of 18 is advised to consult parents and family members, but may not be refused an abortion if she decides to go ahead without doing so, the bill says.
Abortion has divided South Africa for decades, with the conservative white Afrikaner minority most strongly opposing reform.
Current laws disallow abortion except after rape or where there is a clear danger to a woman's mental or physical health and about 1,000 legal abortions are performed in South Africa every year.
But unofficial estimates are that an estimated 120,000 women procure illegal abortions each year.
The proposals were broadly in line with recommendations by a parliamentary committee last year for revision of the long-standing ban.
But the threshholds proposed are significantly more conservative than those put forward by the committee and approved by the cabinet in July.
After weeks of often-acrimonious debate, the multi-party committee suggested abortion on demand for 14 weeks and subject to moderate conditions up to the 28th week.

The cabinet backed the proposal in July, at its first meeting after the June 30 withdrawal of former president F.W. de Klerk's Calvinist National Party (NP) from President Nelson Mandela's unity government.
De Klerk has listed opposition to abortion and a campaign for a return to capital punishment amongst key issues for his party, in opposition for the first time in nearly five decades.

The bill published on Tuesday tightens the conditions under which an abortion can be performed after the 12th week listing physical or emotional risk, rape, sexual abuse and severe social or economic consequences as reasons to allow it.
South Africa's Medical Research Council says close to 50,000 women report to hospitals every year with incomplete backstreet abortions and about 425 of them die as a result.

The bill says men should have no role in a final decision, proposing: "No consent other than that of the pregnant woman, unless she is incapable of giving consent, shall be required for the termination of pregnancy."

The operation must be carried out by a doctor or midwife in a registered facility. If passed into law by parliament, the new legislation will make it a criminal offence to bar anyone access to such a facility.
